title: Other ways of talking about the future

sections.title: On the verge/brink/point of; due to, sure/bound to, set to
sections.content:
Some phrases are commonly used to refer to actions or events in the future with a meaning similar to be about to + infinitive (see Unit 12C). We can use be on the verge of … / brink of … / point of … (+ -ing or noun) to say that something will happen soon:
• People are on the verge of starvation as the drought continues.
• Scientists are on the brink of making major advances in the fight against AIDS.
• Exhausted, mentally and physically, he was on the point of collapse.
Be on the brink of usually refers to something important, exciting, or very bad.
We use be due to (+ infinitive) to say that something is expected to happen at a particular time, be sure / bound to (+ infinitive) to say that something is likely or certain to happen, and be set to (+ infinitive) to say that something is really going to happen:
• The company's chief executive is due to retire next year, but following today's announcement of further losses she is sure to be asked to leave sooner.
• Her new film is set to be a great success.
• 'Will there be somewhere to get a coffee at the station?' 'Oh, yes, there's bound to be.'
There is / are can come before sure / bound to, but do not normally come before due / set to.
Note that we use due to + noun to give the reason for something, not to talk about the future (e.g. Due to fog, all flights from the airport have been cancelled).

sections.title: Verbs with to-infinitive for intentions: aim, guarantee, look (to)
sections.content:
We use some verbs with a to-infinitive to talk about intentions:
• We guarantee to refund your money if you are dissatisfied with the computer.
We can use the present simple + to-infinitive or the present continuous + to-infinitive with the verbs marked * to talk about intentions:
• I aim to get to Bangkok by the end of June. (or I'm aiming to get …)
Some people, particularly in speech and in journalism, use be looking + to-infinitive to mean planning a course of action:
• We're looking to create 3,000 jobs in the city over the next year.
Also: aim*, agree, expect*, hope*, intend*, mean, plan*, promise, propose*, resolve, undertake, want*

sections.title: Past tense forms referring to the future from the past
sections.content:
When the phrases and verbs in A and B are used with past tense forms, they are usually concerned with future events seen from the past (see also Unit 14):
• It was his 64th birthday in 2006 and he was due to retire the following year.
• Nathan had resolved to become fluent in Spanish before he left university.
• The new management had been looking to create 20 new jobs.
• I was aiming to get my book finished by the end of the year.

sections.title: Shall and shan't
sections.content:
Some people use shall (and shan't) instead of will (and won't) in statements about the future, usually with I and we. However, it is more common to use will (particularly its contracted form 'll) and won't:
• He was a good friend and we shall miss him greatly. (more commonly … we'll miss …)
• I'm just going to buy a newspaper. I shan't be long. (more commonly I won't …)
In current English we don't usually use shall / shan't with other subjects to talk about the future, although this is found in formal rules and in older literary styles:
• The match referee shall be the sole judge of fair play.
• All people of the world shall live together as brothers.

exercises.question: The decision of the firm to relocate its international headquarters to Switzerland is ___ questions about the government's new profits tax.
exercises.hint: Emphasis on certainty that questions will be raised → bound to.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: bound to raise
Emphasis on certainty that questions will be raised → bound to.

exercises.question: It seems that other major financial firms are ___ their headquarters out of London.
exercises.hint: Very imminent action → on the point of.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: on the point of moving
Very imminent action → on the point of. The grammatical signals in this sentence — the key words, connectors, or context — require this specific form. Look for these signals to make the same choice independently.

exercises.question: NASA's latest Mars probe is ___ to Earth later today.
exercises.hint: Expected at a particular time → due to.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: due to return
Expected at a particular time → due to.

exercises.question: The probe would be bringing back rock samples that are ___ exciting new information about the planet.
exercises.hint: Almost certain outcome → bound to.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: bound to provide
'Bound to' expresses strong certainty or logical inevitability — something you're almost certain will happen. 'Due to' = expected at a specific time; 'set to' = going to happen (often formal/news); 'on the verge of' = immediately imminent.

exercises.question: The Countryside Conservation Society is ___ a new million-Euro scheme for the protection of endangered plant species.
exercises.hint: Really going to happen (formal announcement context) → set to.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: set to launch
Really going to happen (formal announcement context) → set to.

exercises.question: It is estimated that over 200 species are ___ extinct in the country.
exercises.hint: Certainty of extinction → bound to.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: bound to become
'Bound to' is used when the outcome seems logically inevitable given the circumstances. Compare: 'due to' = scheduled/expected, 'set to' = confirmed plan (often news register), 'on the verge of' = happening very soon.

exercises.question: Sources say the governments of North and South Alicia are ___ an agreement to end their long-running border dispute.
exercises.hint: Very close to a significant agreement → on the verge of.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: on the verge of signing
On the verge of (+ noun or -ing) means something is about to happen very soon. On the brink of is similar but used for important, significant, or potentially dangerous events. Both express immediacy; on the point of is also close in meaning but often more personal.

exercises.question: However, any agreement is ___ resistance from rebel forces in South Alicia.
options: Both sure to face and bound to face
exercises.hint: Either 'sure to' or 'bound to' express certainty — both are correct.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: Both sure to face and bound to face
Either 'sure to' or 'bound to' express certainty — both are correct.

exercises.question: Tennis star Sancho Gómez is ___ a second operation on his injured shoulder.
exercises.hint: Scheduled at a particular time → due to.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: due to undergo
Scheduled at a particular time → due to.

exercises.question: He was ___ tennis earlier this year after a first operation was unsuccessful.
options: on the verge of giving up
exercises.hint: Almost about to quit → on the verge of.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: on the verge of giving up
On the verge of (+ noun or -ing) means something is about to happen very soon. On the brink of is similar but used for important, significant, or potentially dangerous events. Both express immediacy; on the point of is also close in meaning but often more personal.

exercises.question: My computer is now five years old, and I ___ it with a faster one. (look to replace)
exercises.hint: Present continuous is more natural with 'look to' in informal speech.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: am looking to replace
Present continuous is more natural with 'look to' in informal speech. The present continuous shows that the action is temporary or in progress now. Look for context signals: at the moment, currently, today, or a sense of ongoing change or temporary situation.

exercises.question: We haven't completed the work yet, but we ___ it later this week.
acceptable: are expecting to finish / expect to finish (both possible)
exercises.hint: Both present simple and present continuous are possible with 'expect'.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: are expecting to finish / expect to finish (both possible)
Both present simple and present continuous are possible with 'expect'. The present continuous shows that the action is temporary or in progress now. Look for context signals: at the moment, currently, today, or a sense of ongoing change or temporary situation.

exercises.question: I haven't done much work at college so far, but I ___ harder from now on.
acceptable: intend to work / am intending to work (both possible)
exercises.hint: Both forms are correct with 'intend'.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: intend to work / am intending to work (both possible)
Both forms are correct with 'intend'. The present continuous shows that the action is temporary or in progress now. Look for context signals: at the moment, currently, today, or a sense of ongoing change or temporary situation.

exercises.question: We can't provide the spare parts ourselves, but we ___ a supplier who can.
acceptable: aim to find / are aiming to find (both possible)
exercises.hint: Both present simple and continuous are possible with 'aim'.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: aim to find / are aiming to find (both possible)
Both present simple and continuous are possible with 'aim'. The present continuous shows that the action is temporary or in progress now. Look for context signals: at the moment, currently, today, or a sense of ongoing change or temporary situation.

exercises.question: I have passed your letter on to the manager who shall / will reply shortly.
acceptable: shall / will (both possible, will more common)
exercises.hint: With third-person subject, 'will' is standard; 'shall' is very formal/archaic.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: shall / will (both possible, will more common)
With third-person subject, 'will' is standard; 'shall' is very formal/archaic. Use will here — this is neither a fixed timetable event (which would take the present simple) nor a pre-planned personal arrangement (which would take the present continuous or be going to).

exercises.question: Sorry, but I shan't / won't be able to give you a lift after all.
acceptable: shan't / won't (both possible, won't more common)
exercises.hint: With 'I', both shan't and won't are possible; won't is more common today.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: shan't / won't (both possible, won't more common)
With 'I', both shan't and won't are possible; won't is more common today.

exercises.question: I think your parents shall / will be very happy with your decision.
exercises.hint: With third-person subject (your parents), 'shall' is not used for future → will.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: will (third-person → will, not shall)
With third-person subject (your parents), 'shall' is not used for future → will.

exercises.question: Only people over the age of 18 shall / will be eligible to vote in the referendum.
exercises.hint: Formal rule/regulation context — both shall and will are acceptable.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: shall / will (both possible — formal rule)
Formal rule/regulation context — both shall and will are acceptable.

exercises.question: You shan't / won't want to eat your dinner tonight after all that chocolate.
exercises.hint: With 'you', 'shan't' is not standard — use won't.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: won't (2nd person → won't not shan't)
With 'you', 'shan't' is not standard — use won't.

exercises.question: Scientists believe they ___ (be / on the verge of) a major breakthrough.
exercises.answer: are on the verge of making
acceptable: are on the brink of making
exercises.hint: Imminent important event → be on the verge/brink of + -ing.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: are on the verge of making
'Be on the verge of' (+ -ing or noun) means something will happen very soon. 'On the brink of' is similar but usually refers to something important or potentially dangerous.

exercises.question: The report ___ (due / publish) later this month.
exercises.hint: Expected at a particular time → be due to + infinitive.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: is due to be published
'Be due to + infinitive' expresses that something is expected or scheduled to happen at a particular time — like a train or delivery that is expected.

exercises.question: After such poor results, the CEO ___ (bound / face) questions from shareholders.
exercises.hint: High certainty of outcome → be bound to + infinitive.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: is bound to face
'Be bound to' expresses strong certainty or inevitability — you are almost certain it will happen. It's similar to 'be sure to', but with slightly more emphasis on logical inevitability.
